newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin favors debt/GDP ratio below 60 pct.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin favors debt/GDP ratio below 60 pct.

text.p: Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Wednesday he favored cutting Canada's debt-to-GDP ratio to well below the European goal of 60 percent.

"Very clearly there is a range. I have said on a number of occasions that I think that the Maastricht range, at the upper end, is too high, and it wasn't all that long ago, some 20-25 years ago, that we were at 20 percent in this country. And the debate has got to take place within that range," Martin said.
Canada currently has a debt worth about 74.4 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), and the Conservative Party announced on Tuesday it would push for 50 percent in 10 years.
Under the terms of the European Union's Maastricht Treaty, countries which want to join a single European currency should cut their debt-to-GDP ratio to a maximum of 60 percent.
"What is really important is to get the GDP ratio on a steady downward track," Martin told reporters.
"We have now begun that process, and what we have said is that we are not going to deviate from that. We're going to see it going down and it's going to continue to go down."

He repeated his desire for eventual tax cuts but only when health, education and old age pensions are secured. He said the ruling Liberals, likely to call an election this year, would like to give tax cuts to middle and lower-income Canadians.
"But essentially what is really important is not to spend the dividend before it's been earned," he said.
